newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan sacks third provincial government after Bhutto.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan sacks third provincial government after Bhutto.

text.p: Pakistani authorities sacked a third provincial government on Tuesday within eight days after dismissing prime minister Benazir Bhutto, who was preparing for her own legal battle to recapture power.

The governor of the North West Frontier Province dissolved the 83-member provincial assembly and dismissed the coalition government of Chief Minister Aftab Ahmad Sherpao of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
The governor, Mohammad Arif Bangash, acted with the approval of President Farooq Leghari, a government notification said.
It accused the provincial administration of corruption, nepotism and numerous other illegalities.
Bhutto, thronged by chanting supporters, moved out of her official residence into a private home on Tuesday after being sacked on disputed charges of corruption.

"I think this whole thing stinks," an embittered Bhutto told an impromptu news conference at the home of Senator Gulzar Ahmed, where she will temporarily stay with her three children after vacating the prime minister's stately mansion.

About 200 activists from her PPP mobbed the black sedan carrying Bhutto after it passed through the iron gates outside the prime minister's residence on its way to Ahmed's house in the capital Islamabad.

Last week, the PPP government in the southern province of Sindh and an opposition-led coalition government in the southwestern province of Baluchistan were dismissed by provincial governors there on largely similar grounds.

Now, the only provincial assembly that remains to be dismissed is in the most populous Punjab province, where provincial deputies are due to vote on Friday to decide the fate a newly restored anti-Bhutto chief minister under a court order issued before Bhutto's November 5 sacking.
Tuesday's move came as Bhutto's lawyers prepared to file a legal petition on Wednesday asking the Supreme Court to restore her to power.
Sherpao told reporters on Monday that he would go to court if his government were dismissed.

Bhutto's appeal will argue that President Leghari abused his constitutional powers when he dissolved the National Assembly and sacked Bhutto's three-year-old government, a lawyer preparing the brief told Reuters on Tuesday.
Bhutto said on Monday she was confident the Supreme Court would thrust her back into power within a month.
The 43-year-old former prime minister was first ousted in 1990 after 20 months in power. The dismissal order was upheld in court, and Bhutto clawed her way back to power in general elections in 1993.
Bhutto said the court's decision in 1993 to overrule an order sacking former prime minister Nawaz Sharif gave her confidence she would be re-instated.

"If the assembly dissolution with regard to Nawaz Sharif was wrong, the charges against me are even flimsier and the Supreme Court should restore the assembly within a month," she said earlier on Tuesday.

Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government last Tuesday, citing corruption, mismanagement and extra-judicial killings among other accusations which he said had virtually paralysed the government. He set general elections for February 3.
The ousted speaker of the dissolved National Assembly filed a separate legal petition on Monday in the Supreme Court challenging Leghari's order.
Syed Yousaf Raza Gillani argued that Leghari had no right to dissolve the National Assembly as it had been functioning smoothly and there was no constitutional crisis.

Under a controversial amendment to Pakistan's constitution adopted in 1985, the president, who is elected by federal and provincial legislators, has the power to dissolve the National Assembly if he determines that the government cannot function in accordance with the constitution.
